sentences.text: Nobody looks at a weathervane, and that is the entire reason this took two hundred years to notice.
A weathervane is designed to turn.
That is its only function.

It sits on a spindle on a church tower and it turns to face the wind, and if you looked up at it at four o'clock and again at six and it was pointing somewhere else, you would think nothing at all, because that is what it is for.
Femke has tried this on people and it works every time.
She asks them which way the vane on their own church was pointing this morning.
Nobody has ever known.
She asks whether they would notice if it turned while they were watching and they all say yes, and then she asks when they last watched one, and there is a pause.
A weathervane is the most public instrument in a Dutch town and it is the one nobody reads, precisely because everybody has known since they were four exactly what it does.
The cockerel on the Grote Kerk at Nieuwe Sluis is copper, about ninety centimetres from beak to tail, and it went up in 1791 with the tower.

It has been down three times: in 1893 for the spindle, in 1946 for war damage that was not to the cockerel itself but to the mounting, and in 2011 for conservation, when a man from Utrecht took it away for four months and came back with it and a report that is in the church office and that Femke has read.
The report says it is an ordinary copper vane of its period, well made, with a bearing that has been replaced twice, and that it turns freely and is correctly balanced.
Femke's family have been in that town since before the tower.

Her great-grandfather was a wheelwright and her grandfather was a wheelwright until there was no such job and then he was in a factory at Zwolle, and the family has lived in three houses on the same street since 1880 and there is nothing remarkable about that in the Netherlands.
The workshop is a hairdresser's now.

The yard behind it, where the whole of this starts, is a car park with four spaces, and Femke has stood in it and worked out roughly where a man would have been standing in November 1951 to have that view of the tower over the roofline, and it is between the second and third space.
What is in her family, and what Femke did not know about until she was twelve, is the book.
It is a school exercise book with a marbled cover and it is in a drawer, and it has been added to by four people, and the first entry is in November 1951 in her great-grandfather's handwriting.
Each entry is a date, a time, and two compass bearings.
The first bearing is where it was.
The second is where it went to.
That is all.

There is no commentary in the first two hundred entries and no explanation anywhere in the book of what it is for, because the man who started it knew what it was for and assumed that anybody holding it would too.
